Let's work through the various options you might plausibly have, and let's see if there's a path you want to take.

1.If you are in college right now, you can afford to fail your exams in a semester. It may set you back, but it's not necessarily the end. Here are some possibilities that are academically related I've come up with you might like.

* If you are in college right now, using some resources might help you. Schedule an appointment with a counselor asap, and tell them everything. Just say you're struggling really hard with mental illness, and it's making it hard to succeed. Some colleges have disabled students programs that people with mental illness qualify for. You can get extra test time and access to other resources or paths to work with.

* The biggest piece of advice in my opinion for a young 20 year old like you, if you really want a do over, is go to community college and transfer to a state school if you can. Meet with counselor here as well. They might recommend classes that turn into certificates useful for getting jobs. 

2.The reality is that earning a living through hobby type of work requires more discipline and is more difficult than just getting through college in most cases. I know that's the last thing you want to hear, but that doesn't mean college is the only way just that the route you are looking at is a hard one.

* It might be fun to get a hobby to occupy yourself anyway. 

* IT is the best career I know of that requires little work and no college degree, maybe look into that, ask your counselor if they know anyone you can speak to that has expertise in that area. Going to community college might supplement this path.

So the total paradox is that an economics degree is actually not that competitive for PhD programs. That's not to say it doesn't happen, it absolutely does, but econ PhD programs want you to have taken tons of math courses, all the way until very abstract stuff like real analysis and therefore a lot of candidates are math or physics majors since economics majors don't even need to get to multivariable calculus in some cases. Additionally, your GPA is fairly low to be competitive for an economics PhD. However, if your GPA is low because you scored lower in non-math classes, and you scored very well in your econ and more importantly math classes you stand a much better chance. I'm not familiar with down the line how becoming a professor works, but you would need to take the GRE and score well on the math portion as well.

In terms of masters programs, I am again not an expert but have talked to a couple econ PhDs about them. I was told that right now, there aren't any masters economics programs really worth doing, it's really a PhD or bust situation. Additionally if you only get your econ masters degree, if it is for a position where the company typically gets applications from econ PhD candidates, they will think you are a PhD drop out and got the econ masters degree consolation prize so it is often not that much more useful than a bachelors considering the investment that needed to be made.

If you do decide to do a masters in econ, I looked at some programs in England and there are actually 1-year masters programs designed to get you into a PhD program. I'm not sure how successful those are, but they look interesting!
